content:
Japan Tobacco Inc. will book a charge of about ¥1.4 trillion ($8.9 billion) after losing control of its Russian business, the company said on Thursday, in one of the largest single corporate losses yet from Moscow's seizure of foreign-owned assets.

The Tokyo-based maker of Winston and Mevius cigarettes now expects an operating loss of ¥368 billion for the year ending in December, instead of the ¥1 trillion profit it had forecast. It also cut its revenue outlook by ¥63 billion to ¥3.8 trillion. According to [Bloomberg](https://businessmirror.com.ph/2026/11/19/japan-tobacco-hit-by-8-9b-charge-on-russia-seizure/), the company now expects a net loss of ¥724 billion, reversing a previous forecast for a ¥662 billion profit.

The writedown follows decrees signed by Russian President Vladimir Putin on November 5 and 6 that placed all seven of Japan Tobacco's local subsidiaries under temporary administration. The company lost management control and removed the units from its consolidated accounts on November 6. Russia's temporary-administration regime does not formally transfer ownership of the businesses to the state, and Japan Tobacco said it still indirectly owns 100 percent of the affected companies — but without control, it can no longer count their earnings.

What the early coverage has largely left unexplained is what "temporary administration" means in practice for the people and plants involved. The seizure covers four manufacturing plants and a distribution network that made Russia one of Japan Tobacco's most important markets: the country accounted for about 10 percent of group sales and roughly a quarter of adjusted operating profit. Those plants keep running under an administrator appointed by Moscow, but Japan Tobacco has no say in how they are run, what they produce, or where the profits go. For the Russian workers, the change of control is real even if the ownership on paper is not.

The financial damage extends beyond the company itself. The Japanese government owns about 37 percent of Japan Tobacco, making the state its largest shareholder, and the company halved its year-end dividend forecast to ¥68 a share from ¥136. That cut will feed directly into public finances at a moment when Tokyo is already debating tax cuts and new spending. The chairman, deputy chairman and three representative directors will take a 50 percent pay cut for two months, while the representative directors will forgo their bonuses for fiscal 2026.

Investors had already priced in much of the damage. Japan Tobacco's shares have fallen about 25 percent since Russia moved to take control of the assets, and they ended Thursday down 2.16 percent before the profit warning was published. Naoki Fujiwara, a senior fund manager at Shinkin Asset Management, told Bloomberg the size of the loss was close to what analysts had expected — a sign that the market had assumed the Russian business was effectively gone, even before the company confirmed it.

The seizure is also a diplomatic problem, not just a corporate one. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi raised the asset seizures — as well as Russia's arrest of a Japanese journalist — directly with President Putin when the two met in China on Wednesday, on the sidelines of the gathering that brought Trump, Xi and Putin together in Shenzhen, as [Global Wire reported](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/takaichi-putin-first-talks-since-ukraine-invasion-shenzhen-november-2026). It was the first meeting between the Japanese and Russian leaders since the invasion of Ukraine, and the tobacco seizure was evidently high enough on Tokyo's agenda to be raised face to face.

The episode fits a wider pattern that most of the first reports mentioned only in passing. Since the invasion of Ukraine, Putin has progressively tightened the state's grip on foreign-owned businesses that stayed in Russia, using temporary administration as the instrument: the company keeps its name on the register, but control passes to Moscow. Japan Tobacco is one of the largest names to be caught this way, precisely because it chose to keep operating in Russia after 2022 while complying with sanctions — a decision that left it exposed to a market worth a quarter of its operating profit.

That choice is now the central question for other foreign companies still in Russia. Staying preserved revenue and jobs for years, but the seizure shows the exit can be imposed on Moscow's terms, with the loss booked in a single quarter. Japan Tobacco said it would hold a briefing later on Thursday, and investors will be listening for any sign of what, if anything, the company can recover — through negotiation, through the courts, or through the diplomatic channel Takaichi opened in China.

For now, the numbers are stark. A business that delivered a quarter of the group's operating profit is gone from the accounts, a dividend relied on by the Japanese state has been cut in half, and a company that survived the upheaval of the past four years by staying put has learned that staying put was itself the risk. The Shenzhen summit may have produced a joint declaration from Trump, Xi and Putin, as [Global Wire reported](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/xi-trump-putin-summit-shenzhen-november-19), but for Japan Tobacco the week's real news came from Moscow: the largest single loss in its history, imposed by decree.
summary: Japan Tobacco will book a ¥1.4 trillion ($8.9 billion) charge after Russia seized its seven local subsidiaries, swinging the cigarette maker to a full-year loss, halving its dividend and wiping out a quarter of its operating profit.
title: Japan Tobacco hit by $8.9 billion charge after Russia seizes its subsidiaries
